the takeaway: pick a chaotic crossover event people instantly recognize. they know exactly how the classic Coca-Cola and Mentos reaction goes, so when it delivers on a cinematic scale, they stop checking for flaws

single-event physics simulations like this are what seedance 2.5 does best

posts.full_text:
I built a 3D cell where every ribosome fires a protein, then found out Google's AlphaFold server can't fold one ribosome in a single job.

Not because the shape is a mystery. The ribosome is simply longer than the 5,000-token cap the server takes per job.

> READ - one strand of mRNA, three letters at a time
> LINK - one amino acid per codon, onto a growing chain
> RELEASE - the finished chain slides out an exit tunnel and starts to fold

Every protein in the AlphaFold database was built by one of these first.

A human ribosome's RNA alone runs past 7,000 letters, and on the server one letter costs one token.

So the machine that makes every protein is the one you have to cut into pieces before the model will look at it.

Predicting the parts is not seeing the machine. What a ribosome does happens where its parts touch.

People hear that AI solved protein structure and assume the whole cell came with it.

Mapping the ribosome by hand took crystallographers about 20 years and a Nobel Prize.

What the build shows and what it quietly leaves out is in the article below.

https://t.co/bU33O6vL7T

Infinity pool high above the city, man in white sitting on a giant pink flamingo, phone in his hand, skyline stretching out behind him.

What sells it is the order everything arrives in:

→ the flamingo is already resting on the water while the city is still in frame  
→ he stays reclined with the phone before any movement  
→ the float sits right on the glass edge the whole time  
→ the water stays calm while the buildings fill the background  
→ the drop is visible the entire shot

That sequence is what makes the eye accept it. A still of a float on a rooftop is easy. Showing the edge first, the calm float, then the full drop behind is what the clip has to get right.

One pool, continuous view, and the whole thing lands.

Would you have kept him still longer or cut straight to the drop?
